under the feet. No handrail, no human hand and no overhead safety line takes any of it.**

## The scene in question

The kick happens at about **1:57.6** in the video (roughly 1:57.4 – 1:57.8 for the swing and
contact). The on-screen caption for this segment reads **"Balancing on compliant support
(Experiment 4)"**, part of the DLR video *"Passivity-Based Whole-Body Balancing for
Torque-Controlled Humanoid Robots in Multi-Contact Scenarios – Experiments with the Humanoid Robot
TORO"* (Henze, Roa, Ott).

The torque-controlled humanoid **TORO** is standing free, facing the camera, on a **stack of three
layers of soft blue gymnastics mats** — a deliberately compliant, deformable support surface. A man
in a black T-shirt and jeans walks in from the robot's left, swings his leg, and drives his shoe
into the robot **just below the pelvis, on the silver hip-joint housing / upper thigh of the
robot's left hip** (image-right side). A picture-in-picture inset in the top-left corner shows a
floor-level close-up of the robot's two feet on the mats throughout the disturbance.

## What is (and is not) available to take the load

At the instant of the kick the robot has exactly **two contacts with the world: its left and right
foot soles on the gym mats.**

- **The arms are not used.** Both arms hang loosely at the robot's sides with the elbows bent and
  the black three-fingered hands in mid-air. They are not gripping a rail, a wall or anything else,
  and the robot does not reach out to catch itself.
- **Nothing overhead takes the load.** The only thing above the robot is its umbilical cable bundle,
  hung from a green strap on an overhead gantry. Those lines droop in loose, slack catenary loops
  before, during and after the kick — they are never pulled taut, so they carry none of the
  disturbance. The robot is genuinely self-supported.
- **The man does not support it.** He kicks and immediately withdraws his leg and steps back; he
  never puts a hand on the robot to steady it.

So the disturbance wrench applied at the hip can only be reacted against at the ground: the load
path is **hip → thigh → knee → shank → ankle → foot sole → gym mats → floor.**

## What you can actually see bearing the load

- In the close-up inset, both feet stay planted; the **mats visibly compress, crease and bulge up
  around the flat sole plates**, folding into a valley between the two feet. Immediately after
  impact the foot on the kicked side works visibly against the mat — its toe plate presses deeper in
  and the mat sags and re-shapes under it — while the other foot's sole plate digs in on its side.
  The mats are absorbing and transmitting the push.
- The robot's whole-body balance controller **redistributes the contact wrenches between the two
  feet** (and shifts its centre of mass / upper body) to produce the counteracting ground reaction.
  TORO sways for roughly a second, then settles back upright.
- It absorbs the kick **without taking a step, without leaving the mats, and without falling** — the
  point of the demonstration being that the balancer works even when the support underfoot is soft
  and cannot supply a clean, rigid ankle torque.

## Why that is the interesting answer here

Because the support is **compliant**, the feet sink into it and the ankles cannot generate the large
stabilizing torques a rigid floor would allow. The feet and the deformable mats nevertheless carry
the entire destabilizing load, with the balancing controller trading force between the two foot
contacts and moving the body's mass to stay upright.

This contrasts with the other parts of the same video: in the multi-contact experiments TORO puts
**one or both hands onto metal handrails mounted on wooden boxes** — one rail and one hand in
"Redundancy in the wrench distribution" (≈0:17–0:41), two rails and both hands in "Multi-contact
balancing" (≈2:23–3:18). There the load is shared out among three or four contacts, and when the
experimenter disturbs the robot — including standing behind it and pushing down on its hips with
both hands at about 2:49 — the arms and handrails take a substantial part of it. During the **hip
kick on the gym mats, no such upper-body contacts exist**, so the feet and the compliant mat support
alone bear the load.

gemini-cli+gemini-3.8-flash@high.answer:
When the humanoid robot TORO (developed by the German Aerospace Center, DLR) is kicked on its hip while standing in a double-support stance, its destabilizing load is borne and balanced by several closely integrated physical and control components:

### 1. The Compliant Support (Three Layers of Gym Mats)
* **Deformable Ground Surface:** The robot is standing on a highly compliant support consisting of **three layers of blue gym mats** (foam mattress).
* **Load Absorption:** Unlike a rigid floor, this soft support surface physically deforms under the robot's feet during the perturbation. It deforms to absorb, distribute, and dissipate a portion of the impact energy and vertical/shear forces generated by the kick.

### 2. Both Stance Legs and Feet (Double-Support Stance)
* **Double-Support Distribution:** The robot remains in a double-support stance during the kick, keeping both feet firmly planted on the mattress. 
* **Dynamic Weight Shifting:** The lateral kick on the robot's left hip (viewer's right) pushes the robot toward its right side (viewer's left). To counteract the resulting overturning moment, the vertical and horizontal load shifts dynamically. The downward vertical contact force increases significantly on the **right leg/foot** (which is the foot in the direction of the push) pressing it deeper into the mattress, while the load on the left leg/foot is reduced.

### 3. Active Torque-Controlled Joints and Passivity-Based Controller
* **Joint Compliance:** TORO is an actively torque-controlled robot. When kicked, its joint motors do not lock rigidly. Instead, the joints act as a virtual spring-damper system utilizing a **passivity-based whole-body balancing controller**.
* **Torque Adjustment:** The joint torque controllers dynamically adjust to the external perturbation, allowing the robot to "give" compliantly to the kick to absorb its kinetic energy, while generating the precise restoring torques needed at the ankles, knees, and hips to maintain balance on the shifting ground.

### 4. Overhead Safety Tether (Harness) remains Slack
* **Zero Load on the Gantry:** There is an overhead safety harness/tether attached to the top of the robot's head/gantry framework. However, during the kick and the subsequent balance recovery, this tether **remains completely slack**. It does not bear any of the destabilizing load, confirming that the robot is balancing entirely under its own control and physical contact with the mats.

# What bears the destabilizing load at the hip-kick

The hip-kick happens in **Experiment 4, “Balancing on compliant support,” at about 117 to 118 seconds**.

The humanoid robot TORO is standing upright facing the camera with both feet flat on a stack of three thick blue gym mats. A man standing on the image-right side of the frame, on the robot’s left side, swings his right leg up and kicks the robot hard on the outside of **its left hip and upper thigh**, where the silver hip block meets the blue thigh shell. The contact frame shows his shoe pressed directly against that left hip, pushing the robot toward the image-left.

The destabilizing load is borne by **the robot’s two planted legs and feet and the compliant mat stack immediately under them**.

Explicitly:

- Both feet stay fully planted on the top blue mat through wind-up, contact, and recovery. The robot does not lift a foot, step, hop, or shift to one leg.
- The top mat is deeply dented in pits under each foot and sags between them, and the fabric stays furrowed around both ankles. The inset close-up in the upper-left corner shows both soles maintaining full contact while the blue material deforms around them. That visible compression is the support absorbing the kick.
- The arms bear nothing. Both arms remain held slightly out from the torso and the black hands touch nothing before, during, or after the impact.
- The overhead safety rig bears nothing. The green strap and thin wires above the head and shoulders remain slack throughout.
- The man does not catch the robot. After contact he retracts his kicking leg and stands clear while the robot remains upright on the same two footprints.

So the lateral kick on the left hip is transmitted down the stance legs into the deforming blue-mat stack, which compresses under the two feet and carries the destabilizing load while the whole-body balancing controller keeps TORO upright with no extra hand contact and no step.
